text: that report set out very clearly the scale of emissions from a handful of global corporations, and it made the point that the choices of a small number of very large actors dwarf anything that households in this country can do at the kitchen table. I am not saying that as an excuse for inaction. I am saying it because the balance of the burden matters. When we design a carbon tax that lands hardest on the person in a rural constituency who has no bus, no train and no realistic alternative to the car, we are not reducing emissions in any meaningful way. We are simply transferring money out of the pockets of people who have the least capacity to change their behaviour, and we are calling that climate policy. It is not climate policy. It is revenue raising with a green label on it. What would actually reduce emissions in this State is investment, and investment at a scale that this Government has consistently refused to commit to. Retrofitting the housing stock properly, not in a scheme that requires a household to find twenty or thirty thousand euro up front before they see a cent back. Public transport that runs in the evenings and at weekends in towns outside the commuter belt. A grid that can actually take the renewable generation we are capable of producing, because at present we are curtailing wind while importing gas, and everybody in the industry knows it. Supporting the agricultural sector in a way that keeps families on the land rather than driving them off it. Those things cost money and they require planning over more than one electoral cycle, which is precisely why they have not been done. Until they are done, the Government cannot lecture anybody about their carbon footprint, and people know it. They can see the gap between the rhetoric and the delivery, and it is that gap that is corroding public support for climate action in this country.

It could include work with young people who are at risk of being drawn into armed groups, giving them an alternative and a reason to believe there is a future for them at home. It could include trauma counselling and reconciliation work in the aftermath of violence, which is slow, unglamorous work that rarely attracts headlines but which determines whether a peace holds or collapses. The reason I set out those examples is that peacebuilding is sometimes dismissed in this House as a soft category of spending, as though it were something we do when we can afford it. I would argue the opposite. It is among the most cost-effective spending we undertake. The cost of preventing a conflict is a tiny fraction of the cost of responding to one, whether that cost is measured in humanitarian assistance, in peacekeeping deployments or in the displacement of people across borders. Every serious study of this has reached the same conclusion, and yet prevention budgets are almost always the first to be cut because their successes are invisible by definition. On the specific role of faith-based organisations, I would add that they often have something no external actor can buy, which is standing. They are trusted, they were there before the conflict and they will be there afterwards. Our job is to support that work without distorting it, and to make sure that our funding mechanisms are flexible enough for organisations that do not have large compliance departments.

They arrive at these theories because someone offered them an explanation and a remedy at a moment when the system had offered them neither. We have a great deal of experience in this country with frameworks and reporting requirements. They generate documents. They rarely generate outcomes on their own. So I will be supporting the bill, because a framework is better than no framework and because the communities I have spoken to want it passed. There is a real risk that we build a flagship facility in south Wales with components manufactured everywhere except south Wales, and then wonder why the local economic benefit was smaller than promised. That has happened before with major infrastructure in my part of the country and the lesson was not learned. Local content requirements, apprenticeship commitments and procurement designed so that small firms can actually bid are not protectionism. They are the difference between a project in a place and a project for a place, and I would urge Ministers to build them in from the start.

my own county, the local authority once ran the housing programme, the water services, the roads, the fire service and a good deal besides, and it did so with staff who lived in the communities they served and who could be stopped in the street and asked a question. Successive reorganisations have stripped functions away, centralised them into national agencies and left the councillor with a great deal of responsibility and almost no power. That is a bad combination. It produces frustration among elected members, it produces confusion among the public about who is actually accountable, and it produces decisions taken at a remove from the places they affect. If this Bill is to mean anything, it must reverse some of that. Reversing it requires two things that are not in the Bill as drafted. The first is money that local authorities control themselves, rather than money allocated from the centre under conditions that determine how it is spent down to the last line item. A local authority that cannot raise or retain a meaningful share of its own revenue is an administrative office, not a government. The second is staff. We can transfer functions all day long, but if the sanction to recruit is held centrally then the function arrives without the capacity to discharge it, and within two years we will be back here discussing why delivery has been poor. I would also make a point about the executive-elected balance. At present a chief executive can, in practice, decline to act on the settled will of the elected members across a wide range of matters. I understand the history behind that arrangement and I am not naive about why it was introduced. But it has gone too far, and if we are serious about local democracy then the members who face the electorate must be able to direct the organisation they were elected to lead.

We have reflected on that feedback and I am bringing forward amendments today which I hope will address it. The concern raised was essentially that the removal provisions as originally drafted gave insufficient clarity about the grounds on which an arbitrator could be removed and about who bore the cost of any subsequent rehearing. That is a legitimate concern. If the parties to an arbitration cannot predict the circumstances in which the tribunal might be reconstituted, the process loses the speed and certainty that is its principal advantage over litigation, and we would find ourselves having created a scheme that nobody uses. The amendments therefore do three things. They set out the grounds for removal exhaustively rather than illustratively. They require the approving body to give written reasons, which brings the process within the ordinary scope of review. And they make clear that where removal occurs for reasons unconnected with the conduct of either party, the costs of any consequential steps do not fall on the parties. I am grateful to the Institution and to the other professional bodies who engaged with officials on the drafting, and I want to record that their input improved the Bill. I would also say to the House that this is a good illustration of why the pre-legislative process matters. These are technical provisions, they will be operated by practitioners rather than by Ministers, and the people who will operate them are far better placed than we are to spot the point at which a well-intentioned clause becomes unworkable in practice. Where we have not been able to accept a suggestion, officials have written to explain why, and I am happy to place that correspondence in the Library. There remain one or two areas where views differ, in particular on the appointment mechanism, and I expect we will return to those in Committee.

The review recommended that the tax treatment of different forms of work be aligned so that the incentive to misclassify disappears, and it recommended a statutory test that an ordinary person could apply without instructing counsel. Neither has been legislated for. What we have instead is a body of case law built up through individual claimants, usually low-paid, usually without union representation, taking their employer to a tribunal at considerable personal cost and risk, and establishing the point one case at a time. That is a ridiculous way to run a labour market. The consequences fall in a very predictable pattern. The worker classified as self-employed loses sick pay, holiday pay, protection against unfair dismissal, and access to a pension through automatic enrolment. The Exchequer loses the employer contribution. The compliant employer, and there are many, finds itself bidding against competitors whose cost base is lower for no reason other than that they have chosen to characterise the same relationship differently. So this is not only a question of fairness to the individual, although it is that. It is a question of whether we want a market in which the returns go to the firm that organises work well or to the firm that organises paperwork cleverly. Our proposals are straightforward. A single status of worker for everyone other than the genuinely self-employed, with the burden of demonstrating self-employment resting on the party asserting it. Rights from day one rather than after a qualifying period. And an enforcement body with the resources to act on its own initiative, because the current system depends almost entirely on individuals bringing claims, and the people most affected by these practices are precisely the people least able to bring them.

It is built or destroyed by whether the person renting a room at thirty-four, who was told three budgets ago that supply would improve, sees any change in what is available to them. At the moment they do not, and no amount of restating the targets will substitute for that. So let me be specific about what delivery has to mean. It means that the local authorities are resourced to build directly, at scale, with their own staff, rather than acting as a channel through which subsidy passes to the private market. Direct build was how this State housed people for fifty years and we dismantled that capacity in a decade. Rebuilding it takes time, which is an argument for starting immediately rather than an argument against it. It means resolving the cost of construction, because a system in which a modest apartment cannot be delivered for less than the sum currently required is a system that will not produce apartments regardless of how much subsidy we attach. That involves standards, it involves financing costs, it involves levies, and it involves an honest look at productivity in the sector. It means using the land the State already owns rather than disposing of it and then buying units back at a premium. And it means acting on vacancy and dereliction with something sharper than the current incentives, because there are units sitting empty in every town in this country while people on the housing list in those same towns are placed in emergency accommodation forty kilometres away. I support the direction of the budget. I am saying that the difference between this budget and the last several will be measured in output, not in allocation, and that the public has learned to tell the difference.

Under it, we would be bound by a customs territory we could not leave unilaterally, applying rules we did not write, with no vote on how they changed. Whatever one's view of the referendum, that is not a stable position for a self-governing country, and it would not have survived a decade even if it had been accepted. The compromise offers a way through because it accepts the legitimate concerns on all sides. It accepts that there must be no infrastructure at the border in Ireland, which is a commitment I take seriously and which no one in this House should be casual about. It accepts that businesses need certainty and time to adjust, which is why the extended implementation period matters. And it accepts that alternative arrangements, using trusted trader schemes, exemptions for small traders and technology that is already deployed at other borders in Europe, can manage the practical questions. Fiscal capacity is not a moral abstraction, it is an option to act. If the online route becomes the default and the paper route becomes an exception requiring justification, we will have built a system that works best for the people who need it least. The rules must guarantee a paper alternative on request, without the applicant having to prove hardship. The second caution is about open justice. A hearing that takes place through a screen is still a public hearing, and the arrangements for the public and the press to observe it must be designed in from the beginning rather than added after a complaint. The remedy is to remove the parliamentary vote entirely and give the recommendations automatic effect, subject to the commission's procedures being properly followed and to judicial review on that basis alone. I would gently point out that Parliament retains the final word on the rules, the tolerances, the review cycle and the composition of the commission, all of which are legislated for here. What it should not retain is a veto over the application of those rules to particular seats, because that is precisely where the temptation lies and precisely where the public suspects us. The second issue is the tolerance itself. A five per cent quota, rigidly applied, produces constituencies that cross county boundaries, split communities and make no sense to the people living in them. A slightly wider tolerance would allow the commission to respect local ties without any material effect on equality of representation, and most comparable jurisdictions permit it.

First, the advice on which the Government relies has not been published, and this House is therefore being asked to accept a conclusion without seeing the reasoning. State cannot simultaneously be criticised for competing with first-time buyers and criticised for failing to acquire units to prevent homelessness. Those two criticisms have both been made in this Chamber, sometimes by the same Deputies within the same week, and they cannot both be satisfied at once with a fixed stock of housing. That is the honest position and I think the public understands it better than we sometimes credit. Where I do accept criticism is on the composition of what we acquire and how we acquire it. Buying an individual second-hand house on the open market is the most expensive way for the State to add a unit of social housing, and it adds nothing to overall supply. It should therefore be reserved for the situations where it is the right tool, which are principally where a tenant is in situ and facing homelessness, or where a specific adaptation is required for a household with a disability and no suitable new-build exists. Outside those situations, the money is better spent on direct construction, where every euro adds a unit that did not exist before. On the tenant in situ scheme specifically, I have increased the allocation and I have removed some of the administrative conditions that local authorities told me were slowing acquisitions to the point where the notice period expired before the purchase completed. That was an absurd outcome and it should not have taken as long as it did to fix. On the broader point about balance, my view is that the State should be the largest single builder of housing in this country, as it was for most of the last century, and that the current reliance on acquisition and leasing is a symptom of insufficient construction capacity rather than a strategy. Rebuilding that capacity is the work, and it will take longer than one Government.

legislation before us reflects consultation with law enforcement, with victims' organisations and with the provinces, all of whom have to make the system work in practice. I would remind the member that his own party's approach to criminal justice has been consistent for a decade and it has been consistently wrong on the evidence. Mandatory minimum sentences were expanded, they were struck down repeatedly by the courts as unconstitutional, and the practical result was years of litigation, a backlog that let serious cases collapse on delay, and no measurable effect on the offences they were supposed to deter. That is not an ideological claim. It is the record, and it is available to any member who wishes to read the decisions. What actually reduces crime is a combination of things that are less satisfying to announce. It is investment in policing capacity where it is needed, including the forensic and financial crime capabilities that have been chronically under-resourced. It is treatment for addiction, since a large share of property crime traces back to it. It is bail supervision that works, so that judges have an option between release with no conditions and detention. And it is housing and mental health services, because a meaningful proportion of the people cycling through the system are there for reasons that no sentencing provision will address. I do accept that public confidence matters and that in several communities, including in my own province, people do not currently feel safe. That perception is not irrational and it is not created by the media alone. Where repeat offenders are released and reoffend within days, the system has failed and we should say so. Our answer is to address that specific failure through the bail provisions in this bill rather than through a blanket approach that the courts will strike down and that will change nothing while it is litigated.

My concern is what this episode reveals about our general approach rather than about this crisis in particular. We have built an asylum and immigration system whose default assumption is that the applicant is attempting to deceive us, and every process is designed backwards from that assumption. Where public sympathy is overwhelming, as it was here, ministers can override the default and the system proves surprisingly capable of moving quickly. Where public sympathy is absent, the same system grinds people down for years. The people arriving from other conflicts, who have fled comparable violence, encounter the machinery in its ordinary state, and their treatment is the honest measure of our policy rather than the exception we made under pressure. I do not say that to diminish what has been done here. Fiscal stability is not an abstraction that exists in the National Treasury Management Agency. It is experienced by a nurse deciding whether she can afford to keep renting in the city where her hospital is, and by a family whose childcare costs exceed their mortgage. The State has considerable influence over the cost side of the household budget and it has chosen, repeatedly, not to use it. Childcare is the clearest case. In this country a family pays some of the highest fees in Europe for a service delivered by workers earning close to the minimum wage, which is an extraordinary combination and tells you the money is going somewhere other than to the people doing the work or the people using the service. It is going into the cost of premises and into the absence of any public provision to anchor the market. Other countries decided this was a public service and built it. We decided it was a private market and subsidised it, and we have the outcome we designed. The same is true of housing and increasingly of health insurance. If the Government wishes to argue for wage restraint in the public interest, it has to be prepared to act on the costs that make restraint intolerable for the people it is asking. Otherwise the request amounts to asking workers to absorb the failure of policy in their own household budgets, and they will decline, and they will be right to decline.

the current position is that people are prohibited from working for extended periods and are then criticised for not being self-sufficient. That is not an incentive structure, it is a trap, and it produces exactly the outcomes that its critics then point to. Let me address the disincentive argument directly, because it is the only substantive objection and it deserves a proper answer rather than dismissal. The claim is that permitting work creates a pull factor which encourages unfounded claims. The evidence for that proposition is remarkably thin. The comparative studies that have been done, including those commissioned by governments in other European countries with more permissive regimes, do not find a relationship between the right to work and application volumes. What drives applications is conflict, persecution and the presence of existing communities, which is what one would expect. Meanwhile the costs of prohibition are well documented and substantial. People deskill. A surgeon who spends three years unable to practise does not return to the operating theatre easily. Children grow up in households where no adult works, which we know from every other area of social policy has lasting effects. The taxpayer funds accommodation and subsistence for people who would rather be paying tax. Friend the Minister knows all this. I suspect he agrees with a good deal of it privately. Trump has spent years describing journalists as enemies, has sought to use the licensing and regulatory apparatus of the state against broadcasters whose coverage displeased him, and has normalised the idea that unfavourable reporting is by definition fabricated. For a Taoiseach of this country to express sympathy with any part of that framing, in New York of all places, is a serious matter and it deserves a fuller answer than the one offered so far. Let me be fair about the context. The Taoiseach's remarks concerned a specific frustration with coverage of a specific issue, and every politician in this House, including me, has at some point felt that a story was unfair or that a headline misrepresented what was said. That frustration is legitimate and it is human. What is not legitimate is generalising from it to a critique of the media as an institution, because we are not ordinary citizens with a complaint. We hold power over broadcasting legislation, over the funding of public service media, over defamation law and over the regulatory framework. When we speak about the press, we speak as parties with an interest, and the words carry a weight they would not carry from anyone else. The immediate policy context makes this worse rather than better. We have a media sector in serious financial difficulty. Local newspapers have closed. The public broadcaster is in the middle of a funding crisis that this Government has repeatedly postponed resolving. Defamation reform, which the industry has sought for a decade and which affects small outlets most severely, has been promised in three programmes for government. In that environment, ministerial commentary about media bias is not a neutral observation. It is a signal about the seriousness with which those reforms will be pursued. I would ask the Taoiseach to clarify his remarks and to state plainly that he does not share that view of the press.

The mutual aid arrangement between the two services works well in principle and is used many hundreds of times a year in both directions. Where it breaks down is at periods of peak simultaneous demand, which is precisely when it is most needed, because the circumstances that place one service under pressure generally place the other under the same pressure. An ambulance crew waiting with a patient at an emergency department is not available for the next call. When those waits extend to several hours, as they do at certain hospitals on certain days, the effect on the available fleet is dramatic and no amount of additional vehicles will compensate for it, because the vehicles we have are parked outside emergency departments rather than responding. Solving the ambulance response problem therefore means solving the hospital egress problem, which means beds, which means discharge, which means step-down and community care capacity. It is a chain and pulling on one link does not help. That said, there are things within the service itself that we are progressing. Additional paramedics are being recruited and trained, the community first responder network is being expanded, and the clinical hub which allows lower-acuity calls to be managed without dispatching a vehicle is being resourced further. If we end up paying for the completion of forms describing habitat rather than for habitat, we will have added bureaucracy without ecology. Second, the transition. I quote him because I think it is important to acknowledge that the ideas we are debating have a serious intellectual pedigree, and that dismissing them as student silliness is both inaccurate and strategically foolish. If you cannot state the strongest version of an argument you disagree with, you have no business claiming to have refuted it. So let me state it and then say why I reject it. The strongest version runs as follows. A debate is not a neutral space. The participants arrive with unequal resources, unequal platforms and unequal vulnerability to the consequences of what is said. Formal equality of speech in those conditions produces substantive inequality of outcome, and the harms fall predictably on those with least power. There is something in that. Anyone who has watched a broadcast debate in which one participant is discussing an abstraction and the other is discussing their own life will recognise the asymmetry. Where the argument fails is in its remedy, and it fails for a reason that Marcuse himself could not answer satisfactorily. The remedy requires someone to decide which positions forfeit tolerance. That authority, once created, does not remain in the hands of those who created it. It is captured, reliably and quickly, by whoever holds institutional power, and institutional power is not generally held by the marginalised. Every mechanism built to suppress the speech of the powerful has ended up being used against the powerless, in every society that has tried it. That is not a theoretical objection. It is the historical record, and it is why the free-speech position is the radical one rather than the conservative one.

There is no such machine. There is no such dealer network. The charge therefore shifts nothing. It simply removes income from a sector that in this country operates at a median income that would embarrass any Deputy who examined it, and transfers that income to the Exchequer, where it is spent on measures largely benefiting people who do not live in rural areas. The same applies to the proposals on the national herd. Reducing output here, in one of the most carbon-efficient production systems in the world, while global demand remains what it is, results in that production moving to systems with several times our emissions per unit. Members will recall that uptake fell sharply following a coordinated campaign of misinformation directed at parents, and that recovering it required sustained effort by clinicians, by parents' groups and, I want to acknowledge, by a number of young women who spoke publicly about their own experience at some personal cost. On the Deputy's specific proposal for a broader campaign, my hesitation is not about the objective but about the mechanism. Evidence from other jurisdictions suggests that generic public information campaigns have limited effect on the people who are actually hesitant, and can occasionally reinforce hesitancy by drawing attention to a controversy the individual had not previously considered. What works is the conversation between a patient and a clinician they trust, particularly a general practitioner or a public health nurse who has known the family for years. That means the investment is better directed at giving those professionals the time and the materials for that conversation than at national advertising. I am open to being persuaded otherwise if the Deputy has evidence to the contrary, and I say that genuinely. I would add one further point. Vaccine confidence is not primarily a knowledge problem, it is a trust problem, and trust in health institutions is affected by everything else those institutions do. Where people have had a poor experience of the health service, where they have waited years for an appointment or felt dismissed, they are less likely to accept advice from it. Improving general service quality is therefore also a vaccination strategy, though a slower one than any campaign.

Will the Government commit to a full review of every emergency provision, with a presumption of repeal unless a positive case for retention is made and accepted by this House? Not a review that reports at an unspecified point, but one with a deadline and a debate attached. I would add a second point about the precedents that have been set. Regulations restricting fundamental liberties were made under powers designed for something quite different, laid after coming into force, and in some cases debated weeks later. Let me explain why I resist it, since some Members have urged the opposite course. Every time this House legislates on a matter within devolved competence, even where the intention is benign and the outcome popular, it weakens the argument that the institutions matter. It gives every party the option of not participating on the understanding that decisions will be taken anyway, and it teaches the public that the Assembly is optional. Once that lesson is learned it is very hard to unlearn. So I would rather endure the criticism of inaction than accelerate the erosion of institutions that took thirty years and a great deal of suffering to construct. That does not mean the Government has no responsibilities. We have obligations under the agreement, we have obligations in international law, and where a failure to act would leave individuals without rights that this Parliament has determined they should have, that is a different matter and I have said so. The distinction I draw is between the ordinary business of government, which belongs to the Executive, and the framework of rights and obligations, which does not. Reasonable people locate that line in different places and I do not pretend it is always obvious. On the talks themselves, I will not provide a running commentary, for the very good reason that negotiations conducted through the media do not conclude. What I can say is that the parties are engaging, that the issues are well understood by everybody involved, and that the outstanding matters are not primarily technical. They are matters of confidence, and confidence is built through sustained contact rather than through deadlines imposed from London. I remain available to the parties at any hour.

There is precedent for this. Major heritage projects elsewhere in Europe have used exactly this model, and the effect has been to sustain crafts that would otherwise have disappeared entirely. Those skills then serve every cathedral, every listed building and every conservation project in the country for the following generation. I would like to see three commitments in the programme. First, a numerical apprenticeship target, published and reported against annually to this House. Second, geographic distribution, so that the benefit does not accrue solely to the south east, which means using regional workshops for fabrication where that is practical. Third, a commitment that the training is portable and certified to a recognised standard rather than being specific to this project. If we get this right, the legacy of the restoration will outlast the stonework, and that would be something worth the cost.
